And the saying of al-Kumayt:

Abū al-Sammāl read it with a kasra on the final mīm, due to the meeting of two unvowelled letters. And Ḥam is a verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verses 6–9:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And thus the word of your Lord has come into effect against those who disbelieve, that they are the companions of the Fire.﴾ ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with His praise, and believe in Him, and seek forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and admit them to gardens of perpetual residence which You promised them, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants. Indeed, You are the Mighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿"And protect them from evil deeds. And whoever You protect from evil deeds on that Day, You have truly had mercy on him. That is the great triumph."﴾

In the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (Mushaf, the written copy of the Qur'an): "Thus has the word of your Lord preceded." The meaning is: just as I seized those mentioned and destroyed them, so likewise My words have come into effect against all the disbelievers, those who came before them and those who came after, that they are the people of the Fire and its inhabitants.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "kalimat" (words) in the plural. This is also the reading of al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, and Ibn Nisah. The rest read it in the singular, which is for the genus (collective noun). This is the reading of Abu Raja' and Qatadah. All of these are an expression of the sealing of the decree against them. His saying ﴿that they﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "kalimat."

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed of a matter that includes the honoring of the believers and magnifies the hope for them: that the angels who bear the Throne and those around the Throne, who are the most excellent of the angels, seek forgiveness for the believers and ask Allah, Blessed and Exalted, for Paradise and mercy for them. This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, in another verse: ﴿It is a promise binding upon your Lord, sought [of Him]﴾ (al-Furqan 25:16), meaning: the angels asked Him. In this verse Allah explained the general matter (mujmal) in His saying elsewhere: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those on earth﴾ (al-Shura 42:5), because it is known that the angels do not seek forgiveness for a disbeliever. It may be said that the meaning of that is that they seek forgiveness for the disbelievers in the sense of asking for their guidance and, after that, forgiveness for them. On this same basis is the forgiveness sought by Ibrahim, peace be upon him, for his father, and the forgiveness sought by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for the hypocrites.

It has reached me that a man said to one of the righteous: "Pray for me and seek forgiveness for me." He said to him: "Repent and follow the way of Allah, and there will seek forgiveness for you one who is better than me," and he recited this verse. Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: "We have found the most sincerely advising of the servants to the servants to be the angels, and the most deceitful of the servants to the servants to be the devils," and he recited this verse. Jabir ibn 'Abdullah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I have been permitted to speak of an angel from among the bearers of the Throne, whose distance between the lobe of his ear and his shoulder is a journey of seven hundred years."

A group read "al-'Arsh" (the Throne) with a ḍammah on the 'ayn, while the majority read it with a fatḥah.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge.﴾ "Rahmatan" (mercy) is in the accusative as a tamyiz (specificative accusative), and there is an ellipsis in it, its estimate being: they say. Its meaning is: Your mercy and Your knowledge have encompassed all things. This is like their saying: "You have split open with fat (taffa'ta shahman), you have poured forth sweat ('araqan), and you have become pleased in soul (tibta nafsan)." "The way of Allah which is followed" is the sacred laws (shara'i').

The majority of people read "jannat 'adn" (gardens of Eden) in the plural form of "gardens." Al-A'mash, in the narration of al-Mufaddal, read "jannata 'adn" in the singular. It is also so in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him. "Al-'adn" means permanent residence.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants.﴾ It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, in explanation of this: that a man will enter Paradise before his relatives, and he will say: "Where is my father? Where is my mother? Where is my wife?" Then they will be joined to him because of their righteousness, and because of his drawing attention to them and his seeking them. This is the supplication of the angels. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "wa-dhurriyyatahum" (their descendant) in the singular.

[p. 425] His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"And protect them"﴾ — its original form is "awqihim" (protect them); the waw was dropped in imitation of its dropping in the imperfect (future). The alif of connection was dispensed with because the qaf is vowelled. Its meaning: make for them a protection that shields them from evil deeds. The wording may also allow that the supplication is that Allah repel from them the punishment that follows from the evil deeds. In that case, on this reading, there is an ellipsis of a noun in the phrase, as if he said: "and protect them from the recompense of evil deeds."

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called out to: "The aversion of Allah towards you is greater than your aversion towards yourselves, when you were being called to faith and you disbelieved."﴾ ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, You have made us die twice and You have given us life twice, so we acknowledge our sins. Is there any way out?"﴾ ﴿That is because, when Allah alone was invoked, you disbelieved; but when others were associated with Him, you believed. So judgement belongs to Allah, the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, informed of the state of the disbelievers, and placed it after the state of the believers in order to show the difference. It is narrated that this state will be for the disbelievers when they enter the Fire; for when they are made to enter it, they will loathe themselves, i.e., some of them will loathe others, and it is possible that each one will loathe himself, since the expression admits both meanings. "Maqt" (loathing) is contempt and hatred arising from a sin and disgust; this is its definition. When the disbelievers loathe themselves, the angels of punishment will call out to them, by way of rebuke, and say to them: "Allah's aversion towards you in the world, when you were being called to faith and you disbelieved, is greater than your aversion towards yourselves today." This is the meaning of the verse, and this is how Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd interpreted it. Allah, exalted is He, attached the verbal noun to its agent in His saying ﴿the aversion of Allah﴾, and the object is omitted because the context requires it. The lam in His saying ﴿[la-maqtu]﴾ may be the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida') or the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), and the latter is more correct. ﴿[Akbaru]﴾ is the predicate of the subject. The governing element of ﴿idh﴾ is an implied verb whose estimate is: "Maqtakum idh" (your aversion when...). Some scholars estimated it as: "Remember when," but that is weak, as it disrupts the connection of the speech, unless it is estimated that Allah's aversion towards them is in the Hereafter, and that it is greater than their aversion towards themselves; then the implied verb may be estimated as "Remember." It is not permissible for His saying "la-maqtu" to govern it, because the predicate of the subject has come between "al-maqt" and "idh," since "idh" is part of its relative clause, and that is not permissible.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of their saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have made us die twice and You have given us life twice﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Abu Malik said: they meant by their death their being sperm in the loins, then their being given life in the world, then their being made to die the known death, then their being given life on the Day of Resurrection. They said: this is like the verse in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. Ibn Zayd said: they meant that He gave them life as souls (nasam) when the covenant was taken from them at the time they were taken from the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, then He made them die after that, then He gave them life in the world, then He made them die and then He gave them life.

The author, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a weak view, because in it life is given three times.

Al-Suddi said: they meant that He gave them life in the world, then made them die, then gave them life in the graves at the time of the questioning by Munkar and Nakir, then made them die in them, then gave them life at the gathering. This too is subject to the same objection as the view before it, and the first is the most established of the views.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they meant that the disbeliever in the world is alive in body but dead in heart; so their state in the world combined giving life and causing death, then He caused them to die in reality, then He gave them life by resurrection.

The author, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All the disagreement concerning this verse is said about the verse in Surat al-Baqarah. This verse appears to have a meaning cut off from the meaning of His saying ﴿when you were being called to faith and you disbelieved﴾, and that is not the case; rather the two verses are connected in meaning. Their disbelief in the world was also by their denial of resurrection and their belief that there is no gathering and no punishment. Their loathing of themselves only magnified it, because this belief was their lie. So when their loathing of themselves was established and they saw long and wide disgrace, they returned to the matter over which they had disbelieved, which is resurrection, and existence emerged accompanied by their punishment; so they acknowledged it in its most complete form. That is, "We had disbelieved by denying resurrection, and today we acknowledge that You gave us life twice and made us die twice." It is as though they intended to glorify His power, exalted is He, and to seek His pleasure thereby. Then, following this acknowledgement, they said, in hope: "Behold, we confess our sins; is there any way out?" This is like when you require a person to acknowledge a right to you while he denies it; when he sees he is overpowered and defeated, he admits the matter in a fuller way than you had originally asked of him. After their saying ﴿"is there any way out?"﴾ there is something omitted from the speech which the apparent wording indicates, its estimate being: "There is no granting of your request," or something similar of rejection and rebuke.

His saying ﴿That is because﴾ may refer to their loathing of themselves; it may refer to the punishment they are in, or to the restraint, rebuke and humiliation which we mentioned as implied and omitted from mention, the apparent wording indicating it; it may refer to Allah's aversion towards them; it may be that the address with "that" is to the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ in the world; and it may be that it is in the Hereafter, addressed to the disbelievers in general. His saying ﴿when Allah alone was invoked﴾ means: in a state of monotheism and negation of anything else of the gods and rivals. His saying ﴿but when others were associated with Him, you believed﴾ means: when al-Lat, al-'Uzza and others were mentioned, you affirmed and your souls were at rest. So judgement today, with your punishment and your eternal abiding in the Fire, belongs to Allah and not to those whom you used to associate with Him in divinity. "Al-'Aliyy al-Kabir" (the Most High, the Most Great) are two attributes of praise, not in the sense of place, nor in opposition to lowness and smallness.

It is narrated that this state will be for the disbelievers when they enter the Fire; for when they are made to enter it, they will loathe themselves, i.e., some of them will loathe others, and it is possible that each one will loathe himself, since the expression admits both meanings. "Maqt" (loathing) is contempt and hatred arising from a sin and disgust; this is its definition. When the disbelievers loathe themselves, the angels of punishment will call out to them, by way of rebuke, and say to them: "Allah's aversion towards you in the world, when you were being called to faith and you disbelieved, is greater than your aversion towards yourselves today." This is the meaning of the verse, and this is how Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd interpreted it. Allah, exalted is He, attached the verbal noun to its agent in His saying ﴿the aversion of Allah﴾, and the object is omitted because the context requires it. The lam in His saying ﴿[la-maqtu]﴾ may be the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida') or the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), and the latter is more correct. ﴿[Akbaru]﴾ is the predicate of the subject. The governing element of ﴿idh﴾ is an implied verb whose estimate is: "Maqtakum idh" (your aversion when...). Some scholars estimated it as: "Remember when," but that is weak, as it disrupts the connection of the speech, unless it is estimated that Allah's aversion towards them is in the Hereafter, and that it is greater than their aversion towards themselves; then the implied verb may be estimated as "Remember." It is not permissible for His saying "la-maqtu" to govern it, because the predicate of the subject has come between "al-maqt" and "idh," since "idh" is part of its relative clause, and that is not permissible.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of their saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have made us die twice and You have given us life twice﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Abu Malik said: they meant by their death their being sperm in the loins, then their being given life in the world, then their being made to die the known death, then their being given life on the Day of Resurrection. They said: this is like the verse in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. Ibn Zayd said: they meant that He gave them life as souls (nasam) when the covenant was taken from them at the time they were taken from the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, then He made them die after that, then He gave them life in the world, then He made them die and then He gave them life.

The author, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a weak view, because in it life is given three times.

Al-Suddi said: they meant that He gave them life in the world, then made them die, then gave them life in the graves at the time of the questioning by Munkar and Nakir, then made them die in them, then gave them life at the gathering. This too is subject to the same objection as the view before it, and the first is the most established of the views.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they meant that the disbeliever in the world is alive in body but dead in heart; so their state in the world combined giving life and causing death, then He caused them to die in reality, then He gave them life by resurrection.

The author, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All the disagreement concerning this verse is said about the verse in Surat al-Baqarah. This verse appears to have a meaning cut off from the meaning of His saying ﴿when you were being called to faith and you disbelieved﴾, and that is not the case; rather the two verses are connected in meaning. Their disbelief in the world was also by their denial of resurrection and their belief that there is no gathering and no punishment. Their loathing of themselves only magnified it, because this belief was their lie. So when their loathing of themselves was established and they saw long and wide disgrace, they returned to the matter over which they had disbelieved, which is resurrection, and existence emerged accompanied by their punishment; so they acknowledged it in its most complete form. That is, "We had disbelieved by denying resurrection, and today we acknowledge that You gave us life twice and made us die twice." It is as though they intended to glorify His power, exalted is He, and to seek His pleasure thereby. Then, following this acknowledgement, they said, in hope: "Behold, we confess our sins; is there any way out?" This is like when you require a person to acknowledge a right to you while he denies it; when he sees he is overpowered and defeated, he admits the matter in a fuller way than you had originally asked of him. After their saying ﴿"is there any way out?"﴾ there is something omitted from the speech which the apparent wording indicates, its estimate being: "There is no granting of your request," or something similar of rejection and rebuke.

His saying ﴿That is because﴾ may refer to their loathing of themselves; it may refer to the punishment they are in, or to the restraint, rebuke and humiliation which we mentioned as implied and omitted from mention, the apparent wording indicating it; it may refer to Allah's aversion towards them; it may be that the address with "that" is to the contemporaries of Muhammad ﷺ in the world; and it may be that it is in the Hereafter, addressed to the disbelievers in general. His saying ﴿when Allah alone was invoked﴾ means: in a state of monotheism and negation of anything else of the gods and rivals. His saying ﴿but when others were associated with Him, you believed﴾ means: when al-Lat, al-'Uzza and others were mentioned, you affirmed and your souls were at rest. So judgement today, with your punishment and your eternal abiding in the Fire, belongs to Allah and not to those whom you used to associate with Him in divinity. "Al-'Aliyy al-Kabir" (the Most High, the Most Great) are two attributes of praise, not in the sense of place, nor in opposition to lowness and smallness.

(p-428) Allah the Exalted says:

﴿He it is who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky. Yet none takes heed except one who turns back (to Him)﴾. ﴿So call upon Allah, making your religion sincerely His, though the disbelievers dislike it﴾. ﴿Exalted in degrees, Lord of the Throne, He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants, that He may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾. ﴿The Day when they will come forth, nothing of them being hidden from Allah. "To whom belongs the dominion this day?" "To Allah, the One, the Subduer"﴾. ﴿This day every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. No wrong this day. Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾.

This is the beginning of an address concerning the affirmation of Allah's oneness (tawhid) and the clarification of the signs of that. The "signs of Allah" (āyāt Allāh) encompass the signs of His power, the signs of His Qur'an, and the manifest miracles upon the hands of His messengers. As for "sending down provision," it refers to the sending down of rain and to the sending down of decree and judgment, by which a person attains what he gains through trade and other means.

The majority of reciters read "[wa-yunzilu]" with light stress (takhfif), while al-Hasan, al-A'raj, 'Isa and a group read it with doubled stress (tashdid). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Yet none takes heed except one who turns back﴾, means: none takes heed in a manner that is counted and benefits its possessor; for we find that one who does not turn back does take heed, but since that is not beneficial, it is counted as though it did not exist.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So call upon Allah, making (your religion) sincerely His﴾, is an address to the believers, the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). "Call upon" (ud'ū) means: worship (ā'budū).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾, may mean by the "degrees" His sublime attributes, expressed by what is close to the understanding of the listeners. It may also mean: exalted in the degrees that He grants to the believers, and bestows upon His sincere servants in His Garden. "The Throne" ('arsh) is the greatest created body, in which the seven heavens and the earths are like dinars in a desert of the earth.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He casts the Spirit﴾. Ad-Dahhak said: "The Spirit here is revelation, the Qur'an, and other things not recited." Qatadah and as-Suddi said: "The Spirit is prophethood and its station," as He said: ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾ [ash-Shura: 52]. He called it a spirit because by it He gives life to nations and eras, just as the body is given life by its spirit. It is also possible that the casting of the Spirit is general to all that Allah bestows upon His guided servants, in making them understand faith and the rational legal matters. The implied subject, according to this interpretation, is Allah, exalted is He. Az-Zajjaj said: "The Spirit is everything by which people have life; every guided person is alive, and every astray person is like the dead."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by His command﴾: if you take "command" (amr) as a genus of affairs, then "min" (from) is for partition (tab'id) or for the beginning of the end-point (ibtida' al-ghayah). If we take "command" in the sense of speech, then "min" is either for the beginning of the end-point, or in the sense of "bi" (by), and it is never for partition at all.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group read "li-yundhira" with the letter ya' and a kasra on the dhal. In the verb there is a pronoun which may refer back to Allah, exalted is He, or to the Spirit, or to "man" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿whomever He wills of His servants﴾. Muhammad ibn as-Sumayfa' al-Yamani read "li-yundhar" with ya' and a fatha on the dhal and a damma on the mim of "yawm" (day), making the Day the one that warns, by way of expansion (ittisa'). The majority of reciters read "li-tundhira" with ta', addressing Muhammad (ﷺ), and "yawma" in the accusative. Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and a group read "at-talaq" without a ya'; Abu 'Amr also, and 'Isa and Ya'qub, read "at-talaqi" with a ya', and the disagreement over it is like the disagreement that passed concerning "yawm at-tanad". Its meaning is the meeting of all the worlds with one another, which is a matter that did not occur before that Day. As-Suddi said: its meaning is the meeting of the people of heaven and the people of earth. It was also said: its meaning is the meeting of people with their Creator (bari'), and this last meaning is the most frightening of them. It was also said: a person meets his deed.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The Day when they will come forth﴾, means: they will be in an open expanse of the earth, where sight penetrates them and the caller makes them hear. "Yawma" is put in the accusative as a substitution (badal) for the first, so it is in the position of the object; it may also be put in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), with the governing word being His saying, ﴿is not hidden﴾. This is a case-inflection vowel (harakat i'rab), not a fixed-construction vowel (harakat bina'), because an adverb of time is not indeclinable except when it is joined to an unfixed word, as in "yawma'idhin" (that day), and as in the verse of the poet:

"At a time when I rebuked grey hair for youth, and said: 'Will I not yet awaken, while the white hair is a restrainer?'"

And as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿This is a day when the truthfulness of the truthful will benefit them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. As for this verse, the clause is a fully inflected noun-phrase, as you say: "I came on the day when Zayd is governor," so building (the vowel) is not permissible. So consider this carefully.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿nothing of them is hidden from Allah﴾, means: of their inner states, their secrets, and the supplications of their hearts. In the codex (mushaf) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, it reads: [nothing of them is hidden from Him], with a pronoun in place of the written word.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To whom belongs the dominion this day?﴾. It is narrated that Allah, exalted is He, makes this declaration and the world falls silent out of awe and dread, so He Himself answers: ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾. Al-Hasan said: He is the questioner and He is the answerer. Ibn Mas'ud said: He, exalted is He, makes the declaration, and the world answers with that. It was also said: an angel calls out the declaration, and people answer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

When the believer reflects that there is no power or strength for any created being except by Allah, then the whole of time and all the days of the age belong entirely, in dominion, to Allah, the One, the Subduer. But the manifestation of this to the disbelievers and the ignorant becomes clear on the Day of Resurrection. And when one reflects on the subjugation of the people of the heavens and their worship, and on the execution of decree on earth, then what dominion is there for other than Allah?

Then Allah, blessed and exalted is He, informs the people of the place of standing that it is the Day of recompense for deeds, the good and the evil among them. This verse is explicit that reward and punishment are tied to the acquisition (iktisab) of the servant, and that it is a day on which no matter is placed other than in its proper place. So He reckons the creatures in a single moment, just as He provides for them, because He does not need counting or deliberation. There is no lord other than Him. It is narrated that the Day of Resurrection will not reach its midpoint until the believers are admitted into the Garden and the disbelievers into the Fire.

This is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿No wrong this day﴾. Then He informed them about Himself, with swiftness of reckoning, and that is an expression of His encompassing knowledge of things. So He reckons the creatures in a single moment, just as He provides for them, because He does not need counting or deliberation. There is no lord other than Him. It is narrated that the Day of Resurrection will not reach its midpoint until the believers are admitted into the Garden and the disbelievers into the Fire.

(p-428) Allah the Exalted says:

﴿He it is who shows you His signs and sends down for you provision from the sky. Yet none takes heed except one who turns back (to Him)﴾. ﴿So call upon Allah, making your religion sincerely His, though the disbelievers dislike it﴾. ﴿Exalted in degrees, Lord of the Throne, He casts the Spirit by His command upon whomever He wills of His servants, that He may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾. ﴿The Day when they will come forth, nothing of them being hidden from Allah. "To whom belongs the dominion this day?" "To Allah, the One, the Subduer"﴾. ﴿This day every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. No wrong this day. Indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾.

This is the beginning of an address concerning the affirmation of Allah's oneness (tawhid) and the clarification of the signs of that. The "signs of Allah" (āyāt Allāh) encompass the signs of His power, the signs of His Qur'an, and the manifest miracles upon the hands of His messengers. As for "sending down provision," it refers to the sending down of rain and to the sending down of decree and judgment, by which a person attains what he gains through trade and other means.

The majority of reciters read "[wa-yunzilu]" with light stress (takhfif), while al-Hasan, al-A'raj, 'Isa and a group read it with doubled stress (tashdid). His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Yet none takes heed except one who turns back﴾, means: none takes heed in a manner that is counted and benefits its possessor; for we find that one who does not turn back does take heed, but since that is not beneficial, it is counted as though it did not exist.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So call upon Allah, making (your religion) sincerely His﴾, is an address to the believers, the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). "Call upon" (ud'ū) means: worship (ā'budū).

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Exalted in degrees﴾, may mean by the "degrees" His sublime attributes, expressed by what is close to the understanding of the listeners. It may also mean: exalted in the degrees that He grants to the believers, and bestows upon His sincere servants in His Garden. "The Throne" ('arsh) is the greatest created body, in which the seven heavens and the earths are like dinars in a desert of the earth.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He casts the Spirit﴾. Ad-Dahhak said: "The Spirit here is revelation, the Qur'an, and other things not recited." Qatadah and as-Suddi said: "The Spirit is prophethood and its station," as He said: ﴿a spirit from Our command﴾ [ash-Shura: 52]. He called it a spirit because by it He gives life to nations and eras, just as the body is given life by its spirit. It is also possible that the casting of the Spirit is general to all that Allah bestows upon His guided servants, in making them understand faith and the rational legal matters. The implied subject, according to this interpretation, is Allah, exalted is He. Az-Zajjaj said: "The Spirit is everything by which people have life; every guided person is alive, and every astray person is like the dead."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by His command﴾: if you take "command" (amr) as a genus of affairs, then "min" (from) is for partition (tab'id) or for the beginning of the end-point (ibtida' al-ghayah). If we take "command" in the sense of speech, then "min" is either for the beginning of the end-point, or in the sense of "bi" (by), and it is never for partition at all.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group read "li-yundhira" with the letter ya' and a kasra on the dhal. In the verb there is a pronoun which may refer back to Allah, exalted is He, or to the Spirit, or to "man" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿whomever He wills of His servants﴾. Muhammad ibn as-Sumayfa' al-Yamani read "li-yundhar" with ya' and a fatha on the dhal and a damma on the mim of "yawm" (day), making the Day the one that warns, by way of expansion (ittisa'). The majority of reciters read "li-tundhira" with ta', addressing Muhammad (ﷺ), and "yawma" in the accusative. Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and a group read "at-talaq" without a ya'; Abu 'Amr also, and 'Isa and Ya'qub, read "at-talaqi" with a ya', and the disagreement over it is like the disagreement that passed concerning "yawm at-tanad". Its meaning is the meeting of all the worlds with one another, which is a matter that did not occur before that Day. As-Suddi said: its meaning is the meeting of the people of heaven and the people of earth. It was also said: its meaning is the meeting of people with their Creator (bari'), and this last meaning is the most frightening of them. It was also said: a person meets his deed.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The Day when they will come forth﴾, means: they will be in an open expanse of the earth, where sight penetrates them and the caller makes them hear. "Yawma" is put in the accusative as a substitution (badal) for the first, so it is in the position of the object; it may also be put in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), with the governing word being His saying, ﴿is not hidden﴾. This is a case-inflection vowel (harakat i'rab), not a fixed-construction vowel (harakat bina'), because an adverb of time is not indeclinable except when it is joined to an unfixed word, as in "yawma'idhin" (that day), and as in the verse of the poet:

"At a time when I rebuked grey hair for youth, and said: 'Will I not yet awaken, while the white hair is a restrainer?'"

And as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿This is a day when the truthfulness of the truthful will benefit them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 119]. As for this verse, the clause is a fully inflected noun-phrase, as you say: "I came on the day when Zayd is governor," so building (the vowel) is not permissible. So consider this carefully.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿nothing of them is hidden from Allah﴾, means: of their inner states, their secrets, and the supplications of their hearts. In the codex (mushaf) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, it reads: [nothing of them is hidden from Him], with a pronoun in place of the written word.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To whom belongs the dominion this day?﴾. It is narrated that Allah, exalted is He, makes this declaration and the world falls silent out of awe and dread, so He Himself answers: ﴿To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾. Al-Hasan said: He is the questioner and He is the answerer. Ibn Mas'ud said: He, exalted is He, makes the declaration, and the world answers with that. It was also said: an angel calls out the declaration, and people answer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

When the believer reflects that there is no power or strength for any created being except by Allah, then the whole of time and all the days of the age belong entirely, in dominion, to Allah, the One, the Subduer. But the manifestation of this to the disbelievers and the ignorant becomes clear on the Day of Resurrection. And when one reflects on the subjugation of the people of the heavens and their worship, and on the execution of decree on earth, then what dominion is there for other than Allah?

قوله عزّ وجلّ:

﴿وَأنْذِرْهم يَوْمَ الآزِفَةِ إذِ القُلُوبُ لَدى الحَناجِرِ كاظِمِينَ ما لِلظّالِمِينَ مِن حَمِيمٍ ولا شَفِيعٍ يُطاعُ﴾ ﴿يَعْلَمُ خائِنَةَ الأعْيُنِ وما تُخْفِي الصُدُورُ﴾ ﴿واللهُ يَقْضِي بِالحَقِّ والَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ لا يَقْضُونَ بِشَيْءٍ إنَّ اللهَ هو السَمِيعُ البَصِيرُ﴾ ﴿أوَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا في الأرْضِ فَيَنْظُرُوا كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ الَّذِينَ كانُوا مِن قَبْلِهِمْ كانُوا هم أشَدَّ مِنهم قُوَّةً وآثارًا في الأرْضِ فَأخَذَهُمُ اللهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ وما كانَ لَهم مِن اللهُ مِن واقٍ﴾

Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to warn the whole world and to caution them about the Day of Resurrection and its terrors. He meant by ﴿يَوْمَ الآزِفَةِ﴾ (the Day of the Approaching), as Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah said. The meaning of ﴿الآزِفَةِ﴾ is "the near," from "azifa al-shay'" (the thing drew near) when it came close. In the verse, ﴿الآزِفَةِ﴾ is an adjective of a omitted noun whose dread is known and settled in souls, so He expressed it by nearness as a means of frightening. The implied phrase is "the Day of the Hour that is approaching," or "the Great Calamity that is approaching," or something similar. This is like saying, "And warn them of the Hour," in which its terror would be understood from what is fixed in souls about it. Likewise here it is understood when He describes it with the attribute that implies its arrival and imminence.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿إذِ القُلُوبُ لَدى الحَناجِرِ﴾ means "at the throats," as the hearts have risen up from the intensity of terror and anguish. This may be literal on the Day of Resurrection, through the movement of human hearts up to their throats while their lives remain, unlike this world where no one can survive with his heart displaced. It may also be figurative, expressing what a person finds of anguish, the rising of his soul, and the tightening of his throat as the heart ascends. This is like the Arabs' saying: "My soul almost came out." This meaning is experienced by one who is extremely anxious, like one brought near to being killed or the like.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿كاظِمِينَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring either to what the phrase ﴿إذِ القُلُوبُ لَدى الحَناجِرِ﴾ was substituted for, or to what the word ﴿القُلُوبُ﴾ is attached to, since the intended meaning is: "when the hearts of people are at their throats." This is like His saying: ﴿تَشْخَصُ فِيهِ الأبْصارُ﴾ (wherein eyes will stare fixedly) [Ibrahim: 42], ﴿مُهْطِعِينَ﴾ (hastening forward) [Ibrahim: 43], meaning: "wherein their eyes will stare fixedly." The ﴿كاظِمُ﴾ (one who suppresses) is the one who holds back his rage and anguish within his chest.

So the meaning of the verse is that they hope to push back what they find in their throats while the state overpowers them. Then Allah informed that the wrongdoers, those with the wrongdoing of disbelief, are in that state having no ﴿حَمِيمٌ﴾ (intimate friend), that is, a relative who cares for them and takes their side, nor any ﴿شَفِيعٌ يُطاعُ﴾ (intercessor who is obeyed) on their behalf. Even if some of them intend to intercede for others, it is an intercession that will not be accepted. It is narrated that some of the disbelievers will say to Iblis on the Day of Resurrection, "Intercede for us," so he will stand up to intercede, and then a foul odor from him will appear, harming the people of the gathering. Then he will be humiliated, will shrink, and will be disgraced. ﴿يُطاعُ﴾ is in the position of an adjective for ﴿شَفِيعٌ﴾, because the implied sense is "nor an intercessor who is obeyed." The position of ﴿يُطاعُ﴾ may be genitive (khafḍ) following the wording, or nominative (raf') by coordination with the position before the particle ﴿مِن﴾ entered.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

I consider this whole verse, in my view, an eloquent interjected statement within the discourse.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿يَعْلَمُ خائِنَةَ الأعْيُنِ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿سَرِيعُ الحِسابِ﴾ (swift in reckoning) [Ghafir: 17], because the swiftness of His reckoning of creation is only through His knowledge, which requires no reflection or deliberation, nor anything that reckoners need. A group said that ﴿يَعْلَمُ﴾ is connected to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿لا يَخْفى عَلى اللهِ مِنهم شَيْءٌ﴾ (nothing of them is hidden from Allah) [Ghafir: 16]. This is a good view, supported by the harmony of the two meanings, but weakened by the distance between the verses and the large number of intervening words. ﴿الخائِنَةُ﴾ is a verbal noun like ﴿الخِيانَةُ﴾ (treachery), and it may in the verse be an active participle (ism fa'il), as one says "nāẓirat al-a'yun" (the glancing eyes), meaning: He knows the eyes when they betray in their glance. This verse is an expression of Allah's knowledge of all hidden things. Among them is the closing of eyelids, winking with the eye, and a glance that conveys a meaning or that its owner intends a meaning by it. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Sarh came to him to accept Islam after his apostasy, seeking the intercession of ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hesitated with him and then accepted his pledge. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions: "Why did no man stand up to him when I hesitated with him and strike his neck?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, why did you not signal to us?" He, peace be upon him, said: "It is not befitting for a Prophet that he should have treachery of the eyes." In some of the revealed books, there is the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "I am the watcher of resolves, I am the knower of the arena of thought and the winking of eyelids." Mujahid said: ﴿خائِنَةَ الأعْيُنِ﴾ is the furtive glance at what is not permissible.

Then Allah strengthened these reports by saying that He knows what the breasts conceal, of what has not appeared in any eye or otherwise. The exegetes gave an example for this verse: a man looking at a woman who is forbidden to him by marriage or kinship. They said: "The treachery of the eyes is the second glance, and what the breasts conceal" refers to the first glance, which a person cannot prevent.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This example is only a part of the treachery of the eyes.

Then He censured the idols, informing that there is no lord besides Him, who ﴿يَقْضِي بِالحَقِّ﴾ (judges with truth), meaning that He rewards a good deed with ten and a bad deed with its like, and gives the oppressed justice against the oppressor, along with other judgments of truth and justice. The idols judge nothing and execute no command. ﴿يَدْعُونَ﴾ means "they worship." The majority of readers read ﴿يَدْعُونَ﴾ with the letter yā' (yad'ūna), referring to third-person absent, while Nafi' (with a variant from him), Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read ﴿تَدْعُونَ﴾ with the letter tā' (tad'ūna), meaning: "Say to them, O Muhammad: those whom you invoke." Then He mentioned for Himself two attributes from which the idols are clearly devoid; in relation to Allah, exalted is He, these express perception in its unrestricted sense.

Then He referred the disbelievers of Quraysh, who are the referents of the pronoun in ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾, to take lesson from the earlier nations who denied their prophets, whom Allah destroyed. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾ may be taken to be in the accusative position as an answer to the interrogative, and it may be jussive (majzūm) by coordination with ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾. In His saying ﴿كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ﴾, the word ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is the predicate of ﴿كانَ﴾ placed before its subject, and there is a pronoun in ﴿كَيْفَ﴾. This is on the basis that ﴿كانَ﴾ is the incomplete (nāqiṣa) verb. But if it is made complete (tāmma), meaning "occurred" or "happened," then ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is an adverb of circumstance with no pronoun in it.

Ibn ʿĀmir alone read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكُمْ﴾ (stronger than you) with the letter kāf, and it is likewise in the codices of the people of Syria, this being a shift from the absent to direct address. The rest read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهُمْ﴾ (stronger than them), and it is likewise in all the other codices. This is more suitable for harmony with the mention of the absent. ﴿الآثارُ فِي الأرْضِ﴾ (traces on the earth) are the buildings, monuments, and worldly fame. ﴿ذُنُوبُهُمْ﴾ was their denial of the prophets, peace be upon them. ﴿الواقِي﴾ (protector) is the one who shields and prevents, derived from "al-wiqāya" (protection).

قوله عزّ وجلّ:

I consider this whole verse, in my view, an eloquent interjected statement within the discourse.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿يَعْلَمُ خائِنَةَ الأعْيُنِ﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿سَرِيعُ الحِسابِ﴾ (swift in reckoning) [Ghafir: 17], because the swiftness of His reckoning of creation is only through His knowledge, which requires no reflection or deliberation, nor anything that reckoners need. A group said that ﴿يَعْلَمُ﴾ is connected to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿لا يَخْفى عَلى اللهِ مِنهم شَيْءٌ﴾ (nothing of them is hidden from Allah) [Ghafir: 16]. This is a good view, supported by the harmony of the two meanings, but weakened by the distance between the verses and the large number of intervening words. ﴿الخائِنَةُ﴾ is a verbal noun like ﴿الخِيانَةُ﴾ (treachery), and it may in the verse be an active participle (ism fa'il), as one says "nāẓirat al-a'yun" (the glancing eyes), meaning: He knows the eyes when they betray in their glance. This verse is an expression of Allah's knowledge of all hidden things. Among them is the closing of eyelids, winking with the eye, and a glance that conveys a meaning or that its owner intends a meaning by it. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Sarh came to him to accept Islam after his apostasy, seeking the intercession of ʿUthman (may Allah be pleased with him). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hesitated with him and then accepted his pledge. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions: "Why did no man stand up to him when I hesitated with him and strike his neck?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, why did you not signal to us?" He, peace be upon him, said: "It is not befitting for a Prophet that he should have treachery of the eyes." In some of the revealed books, there is the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "I am the watcher of resolves, I am the knower of the arena of thought and the winking of eyelids." Mujahid said: ﴿خائِنَةَ الأعْيُنِ﴾ is the furtive glance at what is not permissible.

Then Allah strengthened these reports by saying that He knows what the breasts conceal, of what has not appeared in any eye or otherwise. The exegetes gave an example for this verse: a man looking at a woman who is forbidden to him by marriage or kinship. They said: "The treachery of the eyes is the second glance, and what the breasts conceal" refers to the first glance, which a person cannot prevent.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This example is only a part of the treachery of the eyes.

Then He censured the idols, informing that there is no lord besides Him, who ﴿يَقْضِي بِالحَقِّ﴾ (judges with truth), meaning that He rewards a good deed with ten and a bad deed with its like, and gives the oppressed justice against the oppressor, along with other judgments of truth and justice. The idols judge nothing and execute no command. ﴿يَدْعُونَ﴾ means "they worship." The majority of readers read ﴿يَدْعُونَ﴾ with the letter yā' (yad'ūna), referring to third-person absent, while Nafi' (with a variant from him), Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read ﴿تَدْعُونَ﴾ with the letter tā' (tad'ūna), meaning: "Say to them, O Muhammad: those whom you invoke." Then He mentioned for Himself two attributes from which the idols are clearly devoid; in relation to Allah, exalted is He, these express perception in its unrestricted sense.

Then He referred the disbelievers of Quraysh, who are the referents of the pronoun in ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾, to take lesson from the earlier nations who denied their prophets, whom Allah destroyed. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾ may be taken to be in the accusative position as an answer to the interrogative, and it may be jussive (majzūm) by coordination with ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾. In His saying ﴿كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ﴾, the word ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is the predicate of ﴿كانَ﴾ placed before its subject, and there is a pronoun in ﴿كَيْفَ﴾. This is on the basis that ﴿كانَ﴾ is the incomplete (nāqiṣa) verb. But if it is made complete (tāmma), meaning "occurred" or "happened," then ﴿كَيْفَ﴾ is an adverb of circumstance with no pronoun in it.

Ibn ʿĀmir alone read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكُمْ﴾ (stronger than you) with the letter kāf, and it is likewise in the codices of the people of Syria, this being a shift from the absent to direct address. The rest read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهُمْ﴾ (stronger than them), and it is likewise in all the other codices. This is more suitable for harmony with the mention of the absent. ﴿الآثارُ فِي الأرْضِ﴾ (traces on the earth) are the buildings, monuments, and worldly fame. ﴿ذُنُوبُهُمْ﴾ was their denial of the prophets, peace be upon them. ﴿الواقِي﴾ (protector) is the one who shields and prevents, derived from "al-wiqāya" (protection).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verse 22–25:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they disbelieved, so Allah seized them. Indeed He is Strong, Severe in punishment.﴾ ﴿And We had certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and Haman and Qarun, but they said, "A sorcerer, a liar."﴾ ﴿So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said, "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women." But the plotting of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿"That"﴾ refers to His seizing them for their sins, even though they had no protector from Him. Then He, the Exalted, mentioned that the cause of their destruction was what Quraysh was upon, namely that a messenger from Allah came to them with clear proofs of miracles and demonstrations, but they disbelieved in him. He mentioned that Allah, the Exalted, seized them, and He described Himself with strength and severity of punishment. All of this is a clarification of a warning to Quraysh.

Then, blessed and exalted is He, began the story of Moses, peace be upon him, with Pharaoh and his chiefs. It is a story in which there is consolation and a model for the Prophet (ﷺ), and in which there is a warning and an example for Quraysh and the disbelievers who oppose him, so that they fear that there may befall them what befell those people of vengeance. And in it is a promise and a hope for the believers of victory and triumph, and praise for the good end of patience. The signs of Moses were many; the greatest of them, and the one he presented by way of challenge, were the staff and the hand. The contest occurred over the staff alone, and then the matter was settled by the faith of the sorcerers and the defeat of the disbelievers.

"Sultan" means proof. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "sulṭānin" with a damma on the lam, while people read it with sukun. Allah, the Exalted, singled out Haman and Qarun for mention, to draw attention to their place in disbelief, and because they were the most famous men of Pharaoh's court. It was said: this Qarun is not the Qarun of the Children of Israel. It was also said: he is that one, but he was attached to Pharaoh as a servant and an assistant who helped him.

His saying ﴿"A sorcerer"﴾ means regarding the matter of the staff, and ﴿"a liar"﴾ refers to his saying: "I am a messenger from Allah."

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed about them that when Moses, peace be upon him, came to them with prophethood and the truth from Allah, these three said, and their opinion was united upon, that the sons of the Children of Israel, the followers of Moses, peace be upon him, and their young men, and those among them with strength, should be killed, and that the women should be spared for service and enslavement. This is a return by them to something like the first killing that had occurred before the birth of Moses, peace be upon him. But this last one did not come to completion for them in its resolve, nor did Allah, the Exalted, help them with anything of it. Qatadah said: this is a killing other than the first, which was out of fear for the newborn. They called those of the Children of Israel we mentioned "sons" just as one says to the clans of a tribe or city and its prominent people: "These are the sons of so-and-so."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"And the plotting of the disbelievers is only in error"﴾ is a concise expression whose strength lies in the fact that Allah, the Exalted, did not enable these three to kill anyone of the Children of Israel, nor did their scheming succeed against them. Rather, Allah led their efforts and their plotting astray.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verses 26–28:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Pharaoh said, "Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land."﴾ ﴿Moses said, "Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿A believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said, "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will afflict you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar."﴾

The apparent meaning of Pharaoh's affair is that when the signs of Moses, peace be upon him, overwhelmed him, his pillar was broken, the beliefs of his companions were shaken, and there was not lacking among them one who disputed his opinion on the matter. This is clear from more than one place in their story. In this verse there are two proofs for this. The first is his saying, ﴿Leave me to kill Moses﴾, for this is not the language of tyrants who are able to enforce their commands. The second proof is the statement of the believer and what he declared, and that his confrontation of Pharaoh was greater than his concealment, and his judgment for the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him, was clearer than his equivocation about the matter. As for Pharaoh, he resorted only to deception, agitation and contrivance. Among this is his saying, ﴿Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord﴾, meaning: "I do not care about the Lord of Moses." Then he returned to his people, showing them counsel and protection for them, and said, ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾. The word "dīn" (religion) here means "authority" (sulṭān), and from this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"If I should dwell in a land of the Banu Asad,
under the authority of 'Amr, and Fadak should come between us..."

Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "wa-an" (and that), while 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "aw an" (or that). Abu 'Ubayd preferred the latter for the addition of the particle. According to the first reading, he feared two things; according to the second, he feared one of two things. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Jahdari, Abu Raja', Mujahid, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Malik ibn Anas read "yuzhira" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the hā', and "al-fasad" in the accusative. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "yazhara" with a fatha on the yā' and the hā', and "al-fasadu" in the nominative, attributing the verb to it. This is the reading of Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, al-A'raj, 'Isa, al-A'mash, and Ibn Thabbat. It is narrated from al-A'mash that he read "wa-yazharu" with a damma on the rā'. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "wa-yazhara" with a fatha on the yā'.

When Moses, peace be upon him, heard the statement of Pharaoh—because he was with him in the same assembly—he called upon his Lord, exalted is He, and said, ﴿Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord﴾, and the rest of the verse. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "'adhtu" with the dhāl clearly pronounced. Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "'udtu" with assimilation (idghām). There is a difference of transmission from Nafi'. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "'ut" with assimilation in the writing.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related the statement of a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, and honoured him with mention, and perpetuated his praise among the nations. I heard my father, may Allah have mercy on him, say: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say from the pulpit—when he was asked to speak about some of the virtues of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all—he lowered his head briefly, then raised it and said:

"Do not ask about the man, but ask about his companion,
for every companion follows the one he keeps company with."

What do you want from a people whom Allah, exalted is He, joined with His Prophet ﷺ, and singled out with his company and receiving revelation from him? Allah has praised a believing man from the family of Pharaoh who concealed his faith, and Allah, exalted is He, placed him in His Book and recorded his mention in the codices, for a statement he made in an assembly of disbelief. Where is he from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who unsheathed his sword in Makkah and said, "By Allah, I will not worship Allah secretly after today"?

A group read "rajlun" with the jīm sukūn, like "'adud" and "'ad'ud," and "sabu'" and "sab'," while the majority read "rajulun" with a damma on the jīm.

People differed about this man. al-Suddi and others said he was from the family of Pharaoh and used to conceal his faith, so "yaktumu" (who conceals) according to this view is in the position of a qualifier without any inversion. Muqatil said he was a cousin of Pharaoh. A group said he was not from the people of Pharaoh but from the Children of Israel, and that the meaning is: "A man who conceals his faith from the family of Pharaoh said," so there is an inversion in the sentence. The first view is more sound, and no one from the Children of Israel could have spoken like this before Pharaoh. It is also possible that he was not of the Copts, and it is said of him "from the family of Pharaoh" since he outwardly followed the religion of Pharaoh and was among his followers. This is like the saying of Arakah al-Thaqafi, lamenting his brother and consoling himself with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

"Do not weep for a dead man after a dead man whom 'Ali and 'Abbas and the family of Abu Bakr have buried,"

meaning the Muslims, when they were under the obedience of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

His, exalted is He, saying ﴿"an yaqula"﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning "for the sake of his saying." This believing man spoke frankly with them in these statements, then he confused them afterwards by placing his speech within the possibility of truth and falsehood, showing them that it was counsel. The nūn of "yakun" was dropped for lightness, according to Sibawayh, and by analogy with the nūn in "yaf'aluna" and "yaf'alani" according to the view of al-Mubarrad, and by analogy with the letters of weakness, the yā' and the wāw, according to the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. He said: It is as though the jussive particle entered upon "yakun," which was already jussive, so the nūn resembled the yā' in "yaqḍī" and the wāw in "yad'u," since its lightness on the tongue is the same.

The interpreters differed concerning His saying ﴿some of what he promises you will afflict you﴾. Abu 'Ubayda and others said: "ba'ḍ" (some) here means "kull" (all), and they cited the verse of al-Qatami, 'Umayr ibn Shuyaym:

"The one who is patient may attain some of his need,
and the one who is hasty may also suffer a slip."

al-Zajjaj said: It is an imposition of proof with the least of what is in the matter, and it does not negate the affliction of the whole. A group said he meant: "Some of the punishment which he mentions will afflict you," and that is sufficient for your destruction. It appears to me that the meaning is: "The one portion of what he promises will afflict you," and that is some of what he promises, because he, peace be upon him, promised them bliss if they believed and punishment if they disbelieved. So if he is truthful, then the punishment is some of what he promised. A group said: By "some of what he promises you" he meant the punishment of this world, because it is some of the punishment of the Hereafter, meaning: "and after that you will return to the remainder," and in "some" there is sufficiency for destruction.

Then this believing man admonished them with his saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar.﴾ al-Suddi said: "A transgressor" in killing. Qatadah said: "A transgressor" in disbelief.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Pharaoh said, "Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land."﴾ ﴿Moses said, "Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾ ﴿A believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said, "Will you kill a man because he says, 'My Lord is Allah,' when he has brought you clear proofs from your Lord? And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; but if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will afflict you. Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar."﴾

The apparent meaning of Pharaoh's affair is that when the signs of Moses, peace be upon him, overwhelmed him, his pillar was broken, the beliefs of his companions were shaken, and there was not lacking among them one who disputed his opinion on the matter. This is clear from more than one place in their story. In this verse there are two proofs for this. The first is his saying, ﴿Leave me to kill Moses﴾, for this is not the language of tyrants who are able to enforce their commands. The second proof is the statement of the believer and what he declared, and that his confrontation of Pharaoh was greater than his concealment, and his judgment for the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him, was clearer than his equivocation about the matter. As for Pharaoh, he resorted only to deception, agitation and contrivance. Among this is his saying, ﴿Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord﴾, meaning: "I do not care about the Lord of Moses." Then he returned to his people, showing them counsel and protection for them, and said, ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾. The word "dīn" (religion) here means "authority" (sulṭān), and from this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"If I should dwell in a land of the Banu Asad,
under the authority of 'Amr, and Fadak should come between us..."

Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "wa-an" (and that), while 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "aw an" (or that). Abu 'Ubayd preferred the latter for the addition of the particle. According to the first reading, he feared two things; according to the second, he feared one of two things. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Jahdari, Abu Raja', Mujahid, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and Malik ibn Anas read "yuzhira" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the hā', and "al-fasad" in the accusative. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "yazhara" with a fatha on the yā' and the hā', and "al-fasadu" in the nominative, attributing the verb to it. This is the reading of Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, al-A'raj, 'Isa, al-A'mash, and Ibn Thabbat. It is narrated from al-A'mash that he read "wa-yazharu" with a damma on the rā'. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "wa-yazhara" with a fatha on the yā'.

When Moses, peace be upon him, heard the statement of Pharaoh—because he was with him in the same assembly—he called upon his Lord, exalted is He, and said, ﴿Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord﴾, and the rest of the verse. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "'adhtu" with the dhāl clearly pronounced. Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "'udtu" with assimilation (idghām). There is a difference of transmission from Nafi'. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "'ut" with assimilation in the writing.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related the statement of a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, and honoured him with mention, and perpetuated his praise among the nations. I heard my father, may Allah have mercy on him, say: I heard Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari say from the pulpit—when he was asked to speak about some of the virtues of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all—he lowered his head briefly, then raised it and said:

"Do not ask about the man, but ask about his companion,
for every companion follows the one he keeps company with."

What do you want from a people whom Allah, exalted is He, joined with His Prophet ﷺ, and singled out with his company and receiving revelation from him? Allah has praised a believing man from the family of Pharaoh who concealed his faith, and Allah, exalted is He, placed him in His Book and recorded his mention in the codices, for a statement he made in an assembly of disbelief. Where is he from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, who unsheathed his sword in Makkah and said, "By Allah, I will not worship Allah secretly after today"?

A group read "rajlun" with the jīm sukūn, like "'adud" and "'ad'ud," and "sabu'" and "sab'," while the majority read "rajulun" with a damma on the jīm.

People differed about this man. al-Suddi and others said he was from the family of Pharaoh and used to conceal his faith, so "yaktumu" (who conceals) according to this view is in the position of a qualifier without any inversion. Muqatil said he was a cousin of Pharaoh. A group said he was not from the people of Pharaoh but from the Children of Israel, and that the meaning is: "A man who conceals his faith from the family of Pharaoh said," so there is an inversion in the sentence. The first view is more sound, and no one from the Children of Israel could have spoken like this before Pharaoh. It is also possible that he was not of the Copts, and it is said of him "from the family of Pharaoh" since he outwardly followed the religion of Pharaoh and was among his followers. This is like the saying of Arakah al-Thaqafi, lamenting his brother and consoling himself with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

"Do not weep for a dead man after a dead man whom 'Ali and 'Abbas and the family of Abu Bakr have buried,"

meaning the Muslims, when they were under the obedience of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him.

His, exalted is He, saying ﴿"an yaqula"﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning "for the sake of his saying." This believing man spoke frankly with them in these statements, then he confused them afterwards by placing his speech within the possibility of truth and falsehood, showing them that it was counsel. The nūn of "yakun" was dropped for lightness, according to Sibawayh, and by analogy with the nūn in "yaf'aluna" and "yaf'alani" according to the view of al-Mubarrad, and by analogy with the letters of weakness, the yā' and the wāw, according to the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. He said: It is as though the jussive particle entered upon "yakun," which was already jussive, so the nūn resembled the yā' in "yaqḍī" and the wāw in "yad'u," since its lightness on the tongue is the same.

The interpreters differed concerning His saying ﴿some of what he promises you will afflict you﴾. Abu 'Ubayda and others said: "ba'ḍ" (some) here means "kull" (all), and they cited the verse of al-Qatami, 'Umayr ibn Shuyaym:

"The one who is patient may attain some of his need,
and the one who is hasty may also suffer a slip."

al-Zajjaj said: It is an imposition of proof with the least of what is in the matter, and it does not negate the affliction of the whole. A group said he meant: "Some of the punishment which he mentions will afflict you," and that is sufficient for your destruction. It appears to me that the meaning is: "The one portion of what he promises will afflict you," and that is some of what he promises, because he, peace be upon him, promised them bliss if they believed and punishment if they disbelieved. So if he is truthful, then the punishment is some of what he promised. A group said: By "some of what he promises you" he meant the punishment of this world, because it is some of the punishment of the Hereafter, meaning: "and after that you will return to the remainder," and in "some" there is sufficiency for destruction.

Then this believing man admonished them with his saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor and a liar.﴾ al-Suddi said: "A transgressor" in killing. Qatadah said: "A transgressor" in disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verse 29–33:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿O my people, to you belongs the kingdom today, dominant in the land, but who will help us against the might of Allah should it come to us?" Pharaoh said, "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct.﴾ ﴿And the one who believed said, "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions,﴾ ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah and 'Ad and Thamud and those after them. And Allah does not intend injustice for the servants.﴾ ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the Day of Calling Out,﴾ ﴿the day you turn back fleeing; for you there will be no protector from Allah. And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾

The saying of this believer, ﴿O my people, to you belongs the kingdom today, dominant in the land﴾, is a means of bringing them down gently and an admonition to them concerning their desires, a warning against the loss of their luxury, and counsel to them regarding the affairs of their worldly life. His saying ﴿in the land﴾ means in the land of Egypt and what adjoins it of their dominion. Then he established for them who is the one who helps them against the might of Allah the Exalted. These statements imply the removal of Pharaoh's awe, and for this reason he submitted and backed down, saying ﴿I show you only what I see﴾, as one who has no authority would say. His saying ﴿Urikum﴾ comes from "ra'a" (to see), which has been made transitive by the hamza, so the verb has two objects: the first is the pronoun in ﴿Urikum﴾, and the second is what is in his saying ﴿except what I see﴾. The sense is as if he said, "I show you what I see." Then he introduced into the beginning of the sentence (p-439) the negative "ma" and reversed its meaning with the affirmative "illa" (except), for restriction and emphasis of the matter, just as you say "Zayd stood," and when you say "Nothing stood but Zayd," you convey his exclusivity and the emphasis of his matter. And "arā" is transitive to one object, which is the pronoun within it referring back to "ma"; its implied form is: "except what I see it," and the omission of this object from the relative clause is good because the relative clause is long.

The majority read "al-Rashad" as the verbal noun of "rashada," while in the recitation of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, [sabil al-rashshad] is read with a doubled shin. Abu al-Fath said: it is an active participle in its form, indicating intensity, and it comes from the triliteral verb "rashada," so it is like 'abbad from 'abada. Al-Nahhas said: this is an error, and he imagined it to be from the quadriliteral verb. His statement, may Allah have mercy on him, is rejected. Abu Hatim said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal used to explain it as "the path of Allah." But this seems unlikely to me regarding Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with him: did Pharaoh claim anything other than that he was a god? And the construction of the word becomes problematic under this interpretation.

People differed regarding the intended meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And the one who believed said﴾. The majority said: it is the believer mentioned earlier, whose statements Allah, blessed and exalted, related up to the end of the verses. A group said: rather, the speech of that believer is ancient, and Allah, the Exalted, intended by "the one who believed" Moses, peace be upon him. This group argued from the strength of his speech, that he openly declared his faith before them, and mentioned the punishment of the Hereafter and other things, whereas the speech of the first was only with flattery toward them.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿like the day of the factions﴾ means: like a day from their days, because their punishment did not occur on one day or in one era. "Al-Ahzab" are those who formed factions against the prophets of Allah, the Exalted, peace and blessings be upon them. The second "mithl" is a substitute (badal) for the first. "Al-Da'b" means custom. His saying ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice for the servants﴾ means: from Himself, that is, He would not Himself wrong them. So the intention here is on its literal footing, because injustice from Him never occurs at all. The meaning of the verse is not that Allah does not intend that some servants wrong others; the proof is that it occurs, and it is impossible that what Allah, the Exalted, does not intend should occur. His saying ﴿the Day of Calling Out﴾ means: a people call out to a people, and the others call out to them.

(p-440) The commentators differed regarding the calling out that is referred to. Qatada said: it is the calling of the people of Paradise to the people of the Fire: ﴿Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], and the calling of the people of the Fire to them: ﴿Pour upon us some water﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], and so on. Another group said: rather, it is the calling that is included in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the day We call every people with their leader﴾ [al-Isra': 71]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: it is the calling that happens among people at the blowing of the trumpet, the blast of terror in this world, when they flee upon their faces because of the terror that seizes them, and some of them call out to one another. This interpretation is also reported from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ). It is possible that the intended meaning is a reminder of every calling on the Day of Resurrection in which there is hardship for the disbelievers and the sinners, and there are many responses to it with a call; among them is what we have mentioned, and among them: "O people of the Fire, eternity without death; O people of Paradise, eternity without death," and among them the calling of the people of treachery, and the call ﴿The hatred of Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 10], and the call ﴿Whose is the kingdom today?﴾ [Ghafir: 16], and other than that.

A group read "al-Tannad" with a sukun on the dal in continuous speech, and this is according to their treating continuous speech like pausal speech in more than one place. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "al-Tanadi" with the ya' both in continuous speech and in pause, and this is according to the original form. The rest read "al-Tannad" without the ya' in both cases. This is also reported from Nafi' and Ibn Kathir. The ya' was dropped together with the alif and lam, following its dropping with what replaces it, which is tanwin. Sibawayh said: the ya' was dropped for lightness. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih, and al-Kalbi read "al-Tannadd" with a doubled dal. This is another meaning, not from "nida'" (calling), but from "nadda al-ba'ir" when a camel flees. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi interpreted this verse according to this meaning. This group related in this sense a hadith: "When Allah, the Exalted, folds up the heavens, the angels of each heaven descend and form rows after rows, encircling the earth on which the people are, for the reckoning. When the world sees the terror of the Resurrection, and Hell extends its neck toward its companions, the disbelievers flee and scatter, fleeing in every direction, and the angels turn them back to the place of gathering, humiliated, having no protector." This group said: the confirmation of this hadith in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, is His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿And the angels will be upon its sides﴾ [al-Haqqa: 17], His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord has come and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass. You will not pass except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33].

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿the day you turn back fleeing﴾ means, according to some of the interpretations of "al-tanad": you flee in terror from the frightening event; and according to others: you flee turning your backs toward the Fire. "Al-'Asim" means the one who saves.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verses 34–35:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you. When he died, you said, "Allah will never send after him a messenger." Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter.﴾ ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any authority having come to them. It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believe. Thus does Allah seal every heart of an arrogant, tyrannical person.﴾

(p-442) We have already mentioned the disagreement regarding all these statements: whether they are from the speech of the believers of the family of Pharaoh or from the speech of Moses, peace be upon him. A group of the commentators, among them al-Tabari, said: the Joseph mentioned is Joseph son of Jacob, peace and blessings be upon him. Another group said: rather, he is his grandson, Joseph son of Ibrahim son of Joseph son of Jacob, peace be upon him. The "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) with which Joseph, peace be upon him, came have not been specified for us, so that we could identify his miracles. It is related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that Pharaoh of Moses overtook Joseph, and that this reproach was directed to him. Ashhab related from Malik that it reached him that Pharaoh lived four hundred and forty years. Another group said: rather, he is a different Pharaoh.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿You said, "Allah will never send after him a messenger"﴾ is a report of the rank of their saying, because they only meant: that there would come after this one someone who claims the like of what he claimed. Those people never acknowledged the prophethood of the first or of the last, nor that Allah sends messengers. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verses 36–40:

The Most High said:

﴿Pharaoh said, "O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾ ﴿to the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses. Indeed, I think he is a liar." Thus was the evil of his deeds made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was turned away from the path. The plot of Pharaoh was nothing but ruin.﴾

﴿The one who believed said, "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct.﴾ ﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence.﴾ ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will be repaid only with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without reckoning."﴾

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentions the saying of Pharaoh when the stratagems had failed him in opposing Moses, peace be upon him, with an argument, and it became clear to all who were present that what Moses was calling to was the worship of the God of the heavens. So Pharaoh called Haman, who was his vizier and the one who managed his affairs, and commanded him to build for him a lofty structure reaching toward the sky. The word "ṣarḥ" (a towering structure) means every great building of exceptional height, and it is derived from manifestness and clarity, and from it come the expressions "ṣarīḥ al-nasab" (of clear lineage) and "ṣarraḥa bi-qawlihi" (he stated it explicitly). It is narrated that Haman fired bricks, which had not been fired before him, and built it to a height of one hundred cubits. Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent Gabriel, peace be upon him, who struck it with his wing and broke it into three pieces: two parts scattered and a third fell into the sea. It is also narrated that Haman was not of the Qibt (the Copts, the native Egyptians), though it was said that he was among them. The word "al-asbāb" (the ways) means the roads; this was said by al-Suddī, while Qatādah said it means the doors. It was also said that the meaning is: perhaps he would find, being near the sky, a means (sabab) by which to reach it.

The majority of readers recited ﴿"fa-aṭṭali'a"﴾ (so that I may look) with the nominative (ḍamm), coordinating it with "abluġu" (I may reach). Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, and al-A'raj recited "fa-aṭṭali'a" with the accusative (naṣb), with the fāʾ as the answer to the expression of wishing (tamannī). When Pharaoh said, in the presence of his chiefs, ﴿"so that I may look at the God of Moses"﴾, his words implied an acknowledgment of the God of Moses, so he corrected this with an uneasy correction when he said: ﴿"And indeed I think he is a liar."﴾
