The majority of readers recited ﴿"and he was turned away from the path"﴾ with a fatḥa on the ṣād, attributing the verb to Pharaoh. Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, ʿĀṣim, and a group recited "wa-ṣuddda" with a ḍamma on the ṣād and a fatḥa on the doubled dāl, coordinating it with "zuyyina" (was made attractive) and treating it as parallel to it. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb recited "wa-ṣidda" with a kasra on the ṣād, meaning "ṣadda", whose original form is "ṣadada"; the vowel was transferred and then the first dāl was assimilated into the second. Ibn Abī Isḥāq and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakra recited "wa-ṣaddun" with a fatḥa on the ṣād, an unpointed doubled dāl, and nunation with a ḍamma, coordinating it with His saying ﴿"the evil of his deeds"﴾. Mujāhid and Qatādah explained it in this sense. The perdition of Pharaoh is evident, for he lost his wealth in the tower and otherwise, he lost his kingdom, he lost himself, and he remained forever in Hell.

Then the one who believed admonished them and called them to follow the command of Allah, the Most High. Then he renounced the world and informed them that it is something enjoyed for a little while, and he encouraged them toward the Hereafter, since it is the abode of settledness. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, Abū Rajāʾ, Shayba, and al-Aʿmash recited ﴿"yadkhulūna"﴾ (they enter) with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the khāʾ. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿraj, al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, and ʿĪsā recited ﴿"yudkhalūna"﴾ (they are admitted) with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the khāʾ.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verses 36–40:

The Most High said:

﴿Pharaoh said, "O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾ ﴿to the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses. Indeed, I think he is a liar." Thus was the evil of his deeds made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was turned away from the path. The plot of Pharaoh was nothing but ruin.﴾

﴿The one who believed said, "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct.﴾ ﴿O my people, this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment, and indeed the Hereafter is the abode of permanence.﴾ ﴿Whoever does an evil deed will be repaid only with its like, and whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided therein without reckoning."﴾

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentions the saying of Pharaoh when the stratagems had failed him in opposing Moses, peace be upon him, with an argument, and it became clear to all who were present that what Moses was calling to was the worship of the God of the heavens. So Pharaoh called Haman, who was his vizier and the one who managed his affairs, and commanded him to build for him a lofty structure reaching toward the sky. The word "ṣarḥ" (a towering structure) means every great building of exceptional height, and it is derived from manifestness and clarity, and from it come the expressions "ṣarīḥ al-nasab" (of clear lineage) and "ṣarraḥa bi-qawlihi" (he stated it explicitly). It is narrated that Haman fired bricks, which had not been fired before him, and built it to a height of one hundred cubits. Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent Gabriel, peace be upon him, who struck it with his wing and broke it into three pieces: two parts scattered and a third fell into the sea. It is also narrated that Haman was not of the Qibt (the Copts, the native Egyptians), though it was said that he was among them. The word "al-asbāb" (the ways) means the roads; this was said by al-Suddī, while Qatādah said it means the doors. It was also said that the meaning is: perhaps he would find, being near the sky, a means (sabab) by which to reach it.

The majority of readers recited ﴿"fa-aṭṭali'a"﴾ (so that I may look) with the nominative (ḍamm), coordinating it with "abluġu" (I may reach). Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, and al-A'raj recited "fa-aṭṭali'a" with the accusative (naṣb), with the fāʾ as the answer to the expression of wishing (tamannī). When Pharaoh said, in the presence of his chiefs, ﴿"so that I may look at the God of Moses"﴾, his words implied an acknowledgment of the God of Moses, so he corrected this with an uneasy correction when he said: ﴿"And indeed I think he is a liar."﴾

(p-444) Then the Most High said: ﴿"Thus was made attractive"﴾, meaning that just as Pharaoh went to extremes in building the tower and engaged in these futile arts, so too the whole of his affair proceeded in this way, and it was made attractive to him, that is, Satan made the evil of his deeds attractive in all his actions. The majority of readers recited ﴿"and he was turned away from the path"﴾ with a fatḥa on the ṣād, attributing the verb to Pharaoh. Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, ʿĀṣim, and a group recited "wa-ṣuddda" with a ḍamma on the ṣād and a fatḥa on the doubled dāl, coordinating it with "zuyyina" (was made attractive) and treating it as parallel to it. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb recited "wa-ṣidda" with a kasra on the ṣād, meaning "ṣadda", whose original form is "ṣadada"; the vowel was transferred and then the first dāl was assimilated into the second. Ibn Abī Isḥāq and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakra recited "wa-ṣaddun" with a fatḥa on the ṣād, an unpointed doubled dāl, and nunation with a ḍamma, coordinating it with His saying ﴿"the evil of his deeds"﴾. As for "al-sabīl" (the path), it is the path of the sharīʿa (divine law) and faith. And "al-tibāb" means loss, and from it comes ﴿"Perish the hands of Abū Lahab, and perish he"﴾ [al-Masad: 1]. Mujāhid and Qatādah explained it in this sense. The perdition of Pharaoh is evident, for he lost his wealth in the tower and otherwise, he lost his kingdom, he lost himself, and he remained forever in Hell.

Then the one who believed admonished them and called them to follow the command of Allah, the Most High. His saying ﴿"follow me, I will guide you"﴾ strengthens the view that the speaker is Moses, peace be upon him, although it is possible that the other could say this too, meaning: follow me in following Moses, peace be upon him.

Then he renounced the world and informed them that it is something enjoyed for a little while, and he encouraged them toward the Hereafter, since it is the abode of settledness. Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, Abū Rajāʾ, Shayba, and al-Aʿmash recited ﴿"yadkhulūna"﴾ (they enter) with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a ḍamma on the khāʾ. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿraj, al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, and ʿĪsā recited ﴿"yudkhalūna"﴾ (they are admitted) with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the khāʾ.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verse 41–45:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And O my people, what is with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire? You invite me to disbelieve in Allah and associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge, while I invite you to the Mighty, the Oft-Forgiving.﴾ ﴿There is no doubt that what you invite me to has no call (to it) in this world or in the Hereafter, and that our return is to Allah, and that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire.﴾ ﴿So you will remember what I say to you. And I entrust my affair to Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of (His) servants.﴾ ﴿So Allah protected him from the evils of what they plotted, and there befell the people of Pharaoh the worst of punishment.﴾

The disagreement has already been mentioned, as to whether this statement belongs to Moses, peace be upon him, or to the believer from the family of Pharaoh. Calling to the obedience of Allah, to His worship and to His oneness is calling to the cause of salvation, so he made it a call "to salvation" by way of brevity and abridgement. Likewise, their calling him to disbelief and to following their religion is a call to the cause of entering the Fire, so he made it a call "to the Fire" by way of brevity. Then he clarified the difference between the two calls, in that the one is disbelief and polytheism, while the other is a call to ascribe oneself to the might and forgiveness of Allah.

His saying: ﴿of which I have no knowledge﴾ does not mean "I am ignorant of it," but rather it means the knowledge that the idols, Pharaoh and others have no share in divinity. No one among mankind has knowledge, by any mode of reasoning, that they have a share in divinity; rather, certain knowledge of their being otherwise, through their origination, is established.

As for "lā jaram": the school of Sibawayh and al-Khalil holds that it is "lā" of negation which entered upon "jaram," and its meaning is: it was established and became obligatory. From this is "jaram" meaning "earned," and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed you struck Abu 'Uyayna a blow, / which Fazara, after it, were bound to be angry" (jaramat Fazara ba'daha an yaghdabu).

That is, it made it obligatory for them and established it for them. So the speech is a negation of the statement that preceded it by "lā," and an affirmation of what follows by "jaram." And "anna" – according to this view – is in the position of a nominative after "jaram," and likewise the second and third "anna." The school of a group of the people of the language holds that "lā jaram" means "lā budda" ("there is no escape") and "lā maḥāla" ("there is no doubt"), so "anna" – according to this view – is in the position of an accusative by dropping the preposition, that is: "there is no doubt that what," and "mā" with the meaning of "alladhī" refers to the idols and what they worshipped besides Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

His saying: ﴿there is no call (to it) in this world﴾ means: no measure and no right by which one ought to be called to it. It is as if he said: "You invite me to that which has no effectiveness, while before us is a grave matter of returning to Allah, the Exalted." And the people of extravagance and polytheism: they are the companions of the Fire by abiding in it and being bound to it. That is: how could I obey you with these realities established, when in obeying you there is abandonment of acting according to them and fear of them? Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid said: "the transgressors are those who shed blood unlawfully." Qatada said: "they are the polytheists."

Then he threatened them that they would remember his saying when the punishment descends upon them; and "sawfa" with "sin" because the matter is open to the possibility that the threat occurs in this world or in the Hereafter. This is the interpretation of Ibn Zayd. Al-Yazidi and others transmitted from Abu 'Amr the vowelling of the "ya'" in [amri] with a fatha. The pronoun in [fawaqahu] may refer to Moses, peace be upon him, or to the believer from the family of Pharaoh. Those who held this said: that believer was saved together with Moses, peace be upon him, and fled among those who fled with him from the followers. ʿĀṣim recited "fawaqāhu" with imāla.

"Ḥāqa" means: descended, and it is used for what is disliked. "Sū' al-ʿadhāb" (the worst of punishment): drowning and what follows it of the Fire and its punishment.

(p-451) The words of the Exalted:

﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind, but most people do not know.﴾ ﴿The blind and the seeing are not equal, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds and the wrongdoer. Little do you reflect.﴾ ﴿The Hour is surely coming, there is no doubt about it, but most people do not believe.﴾ ﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me and I will respond to you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled.﴾

His saying: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. This verse is a rebuke (tawbikh) to these disbelievers who are arrogant. It is as if He, the Exalted, said: the creations of Allah the Exalted are greater and more exalted in worth than the creation of human beings, so none of them has any reason to be arrogant towards their Creator. It is also possible that the speech concerns resurrection and return (al-ba'th wa'l-i'ada). In that case, Allah the Exalted informs that the One who created the heavens and the earth is strong and able to create people again at another time. According to this interpretation, "al-khalq" (the creation) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) added to its object (mudaf ila al-maf'ul). Al-Naqqash said: the meaning is "that which people create," since in reality they do not create anything. So, according to this interpretation, the word "al-khalq" in His saying ﴿than the creation of mankind﴾ is added to its agent (mudaf ila al-fa'il).

His saying: ﴿but most people﴾ implies that a minority among them know this. For this reason, He likened the majority, who are ignorant, to the blind, and the minority, who are knowledgeable, to the seeing. His saying "those who believe and do righteous deeds" is balanced by His saying "the wrongdoer" (al-musi'), which is a generic noun (ism jins) that encompasses all wrongdoers. He, the Exalted, informed that these two groups are not equal, and likewise the ignorant majority of people are not equal to the knowledgeable minority.

The majority of reciters, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-Hasan read ﴿yatadhakkarun﴾ (يَتَذَكَّرُونَ) with a yā' (third person), as an address about an absent party. 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Qatada, Talha, 'Isa and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read ﴿tatadhakkarun﴾ (تَتَذَكَّرُونَ) with a tā' from above (second person), as an address. The meaning then is: say to them, O Muhammad. Then He, the Exalted, affirmed with certainty the information that the Hour is coming. It is the Resurrection, which includes the raising from the graves, the reckoning before Allah the Exalted, and the gathering of people to Paradise and to the Fire. His saying ﴿there is no doubt about it﴾ means: in its own essence and self. Even if some in the world doubt it, there is no doubt in it in itself.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me and I will respond to you﴾ is a verse of grace, favour and promise to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), that their supplication will be answered. This promise is conditional on the will (mashi'a) of whomever Allah the Exalted wills; it does not mean that answering is an absolute certainty for every supplicant, especially for one who transgresses in his supplication. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) criticised the supplication of the one who said: "O Allah, give me the white palace that is on the right of Paradise." Another group said: the meaning of [ud'ūnī] (call upon Me) is [u'budūnī] (worship Me), and the meaning of [astajib] (I will respond) is: with reward and victory. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾. It is also argued for by the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Supplication is worship," and then he recited this verse. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the meaning is: "Declare Me One, and I will forgive you." It was said to al-Thawri: "Call upon Allah, the Exalted." He said: "Abandoning sins is supplication."

Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read ﴿sa-yadkhulūna﴾ (سَيَدْخُلُونَ) with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the khā'. Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan and Shayba read ﴿sa-yadkhulūna﴾ (سَيَدْخُلُونَ) with a fatḥa on the yā' and a ḍamma on the khā'. The reading differs from Abu 'Amr and from 'Asim. "Al-dākhir" means: the humble and abased one.

Another group said: the meaning of [ud'ūnī] (call upon Me) is [u'budūnī] (worship Me), and the meaning of [astajib] (I will respond) is: with reward and victory. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾. It is also argued for by the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Supplication is worship," and then he recited this verse. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the meaning is: "Declare Me One, and I will forgive you." It was said to al-Thawri: "Call upon Allah, the Exalted." He said: "Abandoning sins is supplication."

Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read ﴿sa-yadkhulūna﴾ (سَيَدْخُلُونَ) with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatḥa on the khā'. Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan and Shayba read ﴿sa-yadkhulūna﴾ (سَيَدْخُلُونَ) with a fatḥa on the yā' and a ḍamma on the khā'. The reading differs from Abu 'Amr and from 'Asim. "Al-dākhir" means: the humble and abased one.

(p-453) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿It is Allah who made the night for you that you may rest therein, and the day to see by. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks.﴾ ﴿That is Allah, your Lord, the Creator of all things; there is no god but He. So how are you deluded?﴾ ﴿Thus are deluded those who used to deny the signs of Allah.﴾ ﴿It is Allah who made the earth a place of settlement for you and the sky a canopy, and fashioned you and perfected your forms, and provided you with good things. That is Allah, your Lord. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾

This is a reminder of the signs of Allah, the Exalted, and of lessons which, whenever the intellect reflects upon them, lead it to the Oneness of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and to acknowledging His lordship. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the day to see by﴾, its figurative sense is: "one sees by it," just as you say "a fasting day" and "a standing night." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Creator of all things﴾, means: Creator of every created thing. What cannot be created, such as the Qur'an and the attributes, is impossible to be included in this generality. This is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿which destroys everything﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25], meaning: everything is sent to be destroyed. A group read "tu'faku-na" with a *ta'* (تُؤْفَكُونَ), and another group read "yu'fiku-na" with a *ya'* (يُؤْفِكُونَ). The meaning in the first reading is: "Say to them," and "tu'faku-na" means: you are turned away from the path of reflection and guidance; this is an affirmation in the sense of rebuke and reproach.

Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Thus is turned away﴾, i.e., in this manner and with this attribute Allah diverted the disbelieving deniers of the signs of Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, from the earlier nations away from the path of guidance. Then He explained His blessing, Glorified and Exalted is He, in making the earth a place of settlement and a cradle for the servants, and the sky a structure and a ceiling. The people read "ṣuwarakum" with a *ḍamma* on the *ṣād*; Abū Razīn read it with a *kasra*; and a group read "ṣūrakum" with a sukūn on the *wāw*, after the pattern of *busra* and *busr*.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿of the good things﴾, means: of the pleasant things, in food, clothing, earnings and other things. Whenever the mention of "good things" comes in the context of "provided you with" or similar, it refers to what is pleasant. Whenever it comes in the context of permission or prohibition, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [al-A'raf: 32], and as He said: ﴿and makes lawful for them the good things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157], then "the good things" in such a context means the lawful. On this view the position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding "the good things and the foul things" is derived. The saying of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, that "the good things" are what is pleasant and "the foul things" are what is repulsive, is weak; it is refuted by unlawful pleasant things and lawful repulsive things, against which he has no answer. As for where "good things" occurs alongside "provision," it is merely an enumeration of a blessing in terms of what humans find agreeable, especially in this verse which is addressed to the disbelievers; the blessing enumerated to them is the one they themselves regard as a blessing. The rest of the verse is clear.

﴿He is the Ever-Living; there is no god but Him, so call upon Him, making your religion sincerely His. Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Say: "Indeed I have been forbidden to worship those whom you call upon besides Allah, since the clear proofs have come to me from my Lord, and I have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿It is He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then He brings you forth as a child, then [He sustains you] that you may reach your maturity, then that you may become elders, and among you is one who is taken in death before that, and that you may reach an appointed term, and perhaps you will reason.﴾

Allah Most High's saying:

When the verses listed the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, which demonstrate the corruption of the state of the idols, the clearest of these was that the idols are dead, inanimate objects, while He, Mighty and Majestic, is the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting. The issuing of command from Him, the bringing of things into existence, the management of all affairs, and His knowledge of everything are a decisive proof that He is the Living, there is no god but Him.

His saying: ﴿So call upon Him, making your religion sincerely His. Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ is a connected statement whose implication is: call upon Him, making your sincerity consist of praise. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said with these words: "Whoever says 'There is no god but Allah' should follow its effect by saying: 'Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'" Sa'id ibn Jubayr said something similar and then recited this verse.

Then Allah Most High commanded His Prophet ﷺ to declare openly that he had been forbidden to worship the idols which the disbelievers worshipped besides Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He. The prohibition took effect when revelation and guidance came to him from his Lord, and he was commanded to embrace Islam, which is faith and deeds. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾ means: that I should surrender to the Lord of the worlds and humble myself to Him through obedience.

Then Allah Most High explained the matter of Oneness and Divinity through the lesson in the son of Adam and the gradual stages of his creation. He began with the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, from dust, from clay that sticks together. Thus He made mankind from dust, just as what was born from the one created from dust was produced. His saying: ﴿from a drop of semen﴾ is an indication of procreation from Adam and those after him. The "nutfah" (drop of semen) is the water from which a person is created; the "'alaqah" (clinging clot) is the blood that becomes from the nutfah; and "tifl" (child) here is a generic noun. The "bulugh al-ashudd" (reaching maturity, lit. the peak of strength) has been disputed: it was said thirty; it was said thirty-six; it was said forty; it was said forty-six; it was said twenty; it was said eighteen; it was said fifteen. These last opinions are weak regarding the meaning of ashudd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and among you is one who is taken in death before that﴾ is an expression that recurs in all the stages mentioned. Among people is one who dies before coming forth as a child, others before reaching maturity, and others before old age. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that you may reach an appointed term﴾ means: all these categories are created and facilitated so that each one of them may reach a term appointed for it, which it does not exceed or pass beyond, and so that you may take warning. And perhaps you, O mankind, will reason out the realities when you reflect upon this and contemplate the wisdom of Allah.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 40, verses 68–74:**

His, the Exalted, words:

﴿He it is who gives life and causes death. And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah? How are they turned away?﴾ ﴿Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers. But they will come to know,﴾ ﴿when the shackles are around their necks and the chains, they will be dragged,﴾ ﴿in the boiling water, then in the Fire they will be burned.﴾ ﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where is what you used to associate†﴾ ﴿besides Allah?" They will say, "They have strayed from us. Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before." Thus does Allah lead astray the disbelievers.﴾

(p. 456) His, the Exalted, words: ﴿So when He decrees a matter﴾ is an expression for the bringing into existence, and the bringing forth of the created thing from nothingness. The bringing into being of existing things is by power. The conjunction of the command with this is a manifestation of greatness in the dominion, a subjugation of the created things, and a display of power. The command to the thing brought into being occurs only at the moment power is attached to its bringing into being, not before that, because at that point it is not addressed concerning existence and coming-to-be, and not after that, because what already exists is not told, "Be."

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute﴾, to the end of the verse. Its apparent meaning is that it concerns the disbelievers who disputed about the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Book that he brought, as is evidenced by His words, ﴿those who denied the Book﴾, to the end of the verse. This is the view of Ibn Zayd and the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). Muhammad ibn Sirin and others said: His words, ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute﴾, to the end of the verse, refer to the people of innovative desires (ahl al-ahwa') within the community. This group transmitted a hadith with a similar meaning, and they said: it concerns the people of qadar (the Qadariyya, a theological school that affirmed human power over actions) and those who follow their path. **Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 40, verses 68–74:**

His, the Exalted, words:

﴿He it is who gives life and causes death. And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah? How are they turned away?﴾ ﴿Those who denied the Book and that with which We sent Our messengers. But they will come to know,﴾ ﴿when the shackles are around their necks and the chains, they will be dragged,﴾ ﴿in the boiling water, then in the Fire they will be burned.﴾ ﴿Then it will be said to them, "Where is what you used to associate†﴾ ﴿besides Allah?" They will say, "They have strayed from us. Rather, we did not used to call upon anything before." Thus does Allah lead astray the disbelievers.﴾

(p. 456) His, the Exalted, words: ﴿So when He decrees a matter﴾ is an expression for the bringing into existence, and the bringing forth of the created thing from nothingness. The bringing into being of existing things is by power. The conjunction of the command with this is a manifestation of greatness in the dominion, a subjugation of the created things, and a display of power. The command to the thing brought into being occurs only at the moment power is attached to its bringing into being, not before that, because at that point it is not addressed concerning existence and coming-to-be, and not after that, because what already exists is not told, "Be."

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute﴾, to the end of the verse. Its apparent meaning is that it concerns the disbelievers who disputed about the message of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Book that he brought, as is evidenced by His words, ﴿those who denied the Book﴾, to the end of the verse. This is the view of Ibn Zayd and the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). Muhammad ibn Sirin and others said: His words, ﴿Have you not considered those who dispute﴾, to the end of the verse, refer to the people of innovative desires (ahl al-ahwa') within the community. This group transmitted a hadith with a similar meaning, and they said: it concerns the people of qadar (the Qadariyya, a theological school that affirmed human power over actions) and those who follow their path. The proponents of this view are obliged to treat His words, ﴿those who denied﴾, to the end of the verse, as an independent, separate statement about the disbelievers, with "those who" as the subject, and its predicate being ﴿they will come to know﴾. It is also possible that the predicate of the subject is omitted, and the conjunction "fa" (then) is connected to it.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿when the shackles﴾ mean the Day of Resurrection. The governing element of the temporal phrase is ﴿"they will come to know"﴾. He expressed a future time frame with a term used only for the past, because when the occurrence of the matter is certain, it is fitting to emphasize it by stating it in the form of the past tense. This is common in the Qur'an, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when Allah said, "O Jesus..."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: The chains were not placed around the necks of the people of the Fire because they had overpowered the Lord, the Exalted, but so that they would be dragged when the flames overcome them.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿[wa-al-salasilu]﴾ in the nominative, as a conjunction with [al-aghlalu]. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read [wa-al-salasila] in the accusative, [yashabun] with an open ḥā' and the verb attributed to them, with the verb falling on the chains. A group read [wa-al-salasili] in the genitive, according to the implied meaning: "their necks are in the shackles and the chains," so it is conjoined with the intended meaning of the statement, not with the order of the wording, since its order in the wording is inverted. This is in the manner of the Arabs' saying: "I put the qalansuwa (cap) on my head." In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him) it reads: [wa-fi al-salasili yuthabun]. [Yusbahun] means "they are dragged," and al-sahb means dragging.

"Al-hamim" is the intensely hot, melting water from the Fire, and from it the warm water is called ḥamīm. ﴿Yusjarun﴾: Mujahid said its meaning is: the fire is kindled with them. The Arabs say, "I kindled the oven (sajartu al-tannur)" when they fill it with fire. al-Suddi said, "yusjarun" means "they are burned."

Then He, the Exalted, informed that on the Day of Resurrection they will be made to stand in a manner of rebuke and reproach, and it will be said to them: "Where are the idols you used to worship in the world?" They will say: "They have strayed from us," meaning they have fallen into the Fire, disappeared, and vanished. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verses 75–78:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿That is because you used to exult in the land without right, and because you used to be insolent.﴾ ﴿Enter the gates of Hell, abiding therein. Wretched is the abode of the arrogant.﴾ ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true. And whether We show you part of what We promise them or We take you [in death] – to Us they will be returned.﴾ ﴿And We have already sent messengers before you; among them are those We have related to you, and among them are those We have not related to you. And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah. So when the command of Allah comes, it will be concluded in truth, and the falsifiers will lose everything at that time.﴾

The meaning: It is said to the disbelievers who are being punished: "That is the punishment you are in, because you used to exult in the world through sins and disbelief, and you used to be insolent." Mujahid said: its meaning is ostentatious pride (al-ashar) and exultation (al-batar). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: boasting (al-fakhr) and conceit (al-khuyala').

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿[Enter]﴾ means: it will be said to them before this dialogue, at the very beginning: "Enter," because this address comes only after their entry, at the time when the shackles are on their necks. The gates of Hell are the seven that lead to its levels (tabaqat) and its seven strata (adraak). "Al-mathwa" is the place of residence.

Then Allah, the Exalted, consoled His Prophet ﷺ and promised him with His saying: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾, concerning your victory and the manifestation of your affair. That is a matter of which you may see part during your life, so your eye will be comforted by it, or you may die before that. Then to Our command and Our punishment they will go and return. The majority of readers recited "[yurja'un]" with a damma on the yā'; Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Ya'qub recited [yurja'un] with a fatha on the yā'; Talha ibn Musarrif and Ya'qub, in the narration of al-Walid ibn Hassan, recited [turja'un] with a fatha on the tā', dotted from above.

(p-458) His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We have already sent messengers before you﴾, the verse is a refutation of the Arabs who said that Allah does not send a human being as a messenger, and who deemed that unlikely. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿among them are those We have related to you﴾, al-Naqqash said: they are twenty-four. His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and among them are those We have not related to you﴾ has been narrated through Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, sent eight thousand messengers." It has also been narrated from Salman, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who said: "Allah sent four thousand prophets." It has also been narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Allah sent a messenger from Abyssinia, black," and he is the one who was not related to Muhammad ﷺ.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is what he cited to show that this Abyssinian is an example of those not related, not that he alone is the one intended, for that is far-fetched.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And it was not for a messenger﴾ is a refutation of the Quraysh in their denial of the affair of Muhammad ﷺ and their saying that he lies about Allah, the Exalted. Permission (idhn) implies knowledge and empowerment, and when a command is attached to it, it grows strong, as is the case in the sending of a prophet. Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾, meaning: when Allah wills to send a messenger and raise a prophet, He decrees that and executes it in truth, and every falsifier loses, and comes to corruption in his hereafter. The verse may also bear another meaning, namely that by "the command of Allah" is intended the Resurrection, so the verse would be a warning to them.

**The Almighty's words:**

﴿It is Allah who made the livestock for you, that you may ride some of them and of them you eat.﴾ ﴿And for you in them are benefits, and that you may reach by them a need in your breasts, and upon them and upon the ships you are carried.﴾ ﴿And He shows you His signs, so which of the signs of Allah do you deny?﴾ ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them? They were more numerous than them and greater in strength and in traces upon the earth, but what they used to earn did not avail them.﴾

These are verses of lessons and an enumeration of blessings. "Al-Anʿām" (the livestock) refers to the eight pairs. The "minhā" (of them) in the first place is partitive (*li-l-tabʿīḍ*), because what is mentioned is not all livestock but camels in particular. The second "minhā" is for explaining the kind (*li-bayān al-jins*), because all of them are eaten. Al-Ṭabarī said regarding this verse that *al-anʿām* includes camels, cattle, sheep, horses, mules, donkeys and other beasts from which benefit is derived, so "minhā" in both places is partitive according to this view. However, this is a weak opinion. Rather, *al-anʿām* refers only to the eight pairs that Allah mentioned. Then the Exalted mentioned the benefits in a general way, because they are too numerous to be counted.

As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿and that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾, it means crossing the long deserts and the distant hardships. "Al-fulk" (ships) here is a plural. "Tuḥmalūn" (you are carried) means by land and by sea. The Exalted mentioned being carried upon them, although riding them was mentioned earlier, because the meaning differs between the two matters and there is a distinction between them. Riding is what is customary for short distances and is used for towns and settled places, so it is the counterpart of eating from them and the rest of the benefits. Then after that He specified the longer journey and the needs of the breasts together with distance, and this is the carrying which He paired with its like in the matter of ships.

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned His signs in a general way, comprehensive of every lesson and point of reflection. This is not confined, due to its breadth, and because in everything there is a sign that indicates His oneness. Then He confirmed them, in the manner of rebuke, by His words: ﴿so which of the signs of Allah do you deny?﴾

Then the Exalted argued against Quraysh by what appears among the earlier nations of the punishments of Allah upon the disbelievers, who were more numerous, greater in bodily strength and in dominions, and more mighty in構 buildings and deeds than Quraysh and the Arabs. Their earnings and their condition did not avail them anything when the punishment of Allah and His seizing came upon them. The "mā" in His words ﴿fa-mā aghnā﴾ (but what... did not avail) is negative. Al-Ṭabarī said: it has also been said that it is an interrogative of reproach and confirmation.

These are verses of lessons and an enumeration of blessings. "Al-Anʿām" (the livestock) refers to the eight pairs. The "minhā" (of them) in the first place is partitive (*li-l-tabʿīḍ*), because what is mentioned is not all livestock but camels in particular. The second "minhā" is for explaining the kind (*li-bayān al-jins*), because all of them are eaten. Al-Ṭabarī said regarding this verse that *al-anʿām* includes camels, cattle, sheep, horses, mules, donkeys and other beasts from which benefit is derived, so "minhā" in both places is partitive according to this view. However, this is a weak opinion. Rather, *al-anʿām* refers only to the eight pairs that Allah mentioned. Then the Exalted mentioned the benefits in a general way, because they are too numerous to be counted.

As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿and that you may reach by them a need in your breasts﴾, it means crossing the long deserts and the distant hardships. "Al-fulk" (ships) here is a plural. "Tuḥmalūn" (you are carried) means by land and by sea. The Exalted mentioned being carried upon them, although riding them was mentioned earlier, because the meaning differs between the two matters and there is a distinction between them. Riding is what is customary for short distances and is used for towns and settled places, so it is the counterpart of eating from them and the rest of the benefits. Then after that He specified the longer journey and the needs of the breasts together with distance, and this is the carrying which He paired with its like in the matter of ships.

Then Allah, the Exalted, mentioned His signs in a general way, comprehensive of every lesson and point of reflection. This is not confined, due to its breadth, and because in everything there is a sign that indicates His oneness. Then He confirmed them, in the manner of rebuke, by His words: ﴿so which of the signs of Allah do you deny?﴾

Then the Exalted argued against Quraysh by what appears among the earlier nations of the punishments of Allah upon the disbelievers, who were more numerous, greater in bodily strength and in dominions, and more mighty in構 buildings and deeds than Quraysh and the Arabs. Their earnings and their condition did not avail them anything when the punishment of Allah and His seizing came upon them. The "mā" in His words ﴿fa-mā aghnā﴾ (but what... did not avail) is negative. Al-Ṭabarī said: it has also been said that it is an interrogative of reproach and confirmation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 40, verses 83–85:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they rejoiced in what knowledge they had, and there encompassed them that which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Then, when they saw Our punishment, they said, "We believe in Allah alone, and we reject what we used to associate with Him."﴾ ﴿But their faith was not going to benefit them when they saw Our punishment. This is the way of Allah which has passed before among His servants. And there the disbelievers were lost.﴾

The pronoun in ﴿came to them﴾ refers to the nations mentioned, who were made an example and a lesson (p-460).

The exegetes differed over whom the pronoun in ﴿"they rejoiced"﴾ refers to. Mujahid and others said: it refers to the nations mentioned, meaning: they rejoiced in what knowledge they had according to their own assumption and belief that they would not be resurrected and would not be brought to account. Ibn Zayd said: they were deceived by their knowledge of worldly affairs and livelihoods, and they assumed that there is no Hereafter, so they rejoiced. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ [al-Rum: 7]. Another group said: the pronoun in "rejoiced" refers to the messengers. In this interpretation there is an ellipsis, and its estimate is: "they denied them, so they [i.e., the messengers] rejoiced in what knowledge they had of Allah, and in their trust in Him and in His victory for them."

"Haqa" means: it descended and was fixed, and it is used for evil. The "ma" in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿what they used to⦆ — the "ma" in ﴿ma kanu bihi﴾ refers to the punishment, which they used to deny and whose matter they used to mock. The pronoun in "bihim" refers to the disbelievers without any dispute.

Then He related the condition of some of them who believed after the punishment had already overtaken them, and that did not benefit them. In mentioning this there is an exhortation to the Arabs to hasten, and a warning against delay, lest a punishment overtake them for which repentance will not benefit them after it has overtaken them. As for the story of the people of Yunus, peace be upon him, they saw the punishment but it had not yet overtaken them; its exegesis has passed in full detail in the surah of Yunus, peace be upon him. "Sunnata" is in the accusative as a verbal noun. "Khalat" means: it passed, continued, and became a custom. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"Hunalika"﴾ is a reference to the times of punishment, meaning: their loss became manifest and the recompense of their disbelief arrived.

The commentary of Surah Ghafir is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
